newsitem.title: CANADA: Peru rebels in for long haul - Canada ex-hostage.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels in for long haul - Canada ex-hostage.

text.p: Calm and patience are needed to deal with the Peruvian hostage crisis because the guerrillas are prepared to hold out a long time, former captive Anthony Vincent, Canada's ambassador to Peru, said on Thursday.
"They obviously have a lot of endurance, they're very well-disciplined, well-organized, very well-armed," Vincent said during a visit to Canada to report on the situation in Lima.
"I think they're prepared to wait quite a long time if they need to...Above anything else calmness and patience are what are going to be necessary over the next few days or weeks," he told reporters.
Vincent and his wife were among the 500 hostages initially seized by leftist Tupac Amaru guerrillas when they stormed a party at the Japanese ambassador's residence on December 17.
The women were freed within hours, and Vincent was allowed to leave the next day to help in mediation efforts, a role the Red Cross eventually took over.
Vincent, an anti-terrorism expert serving as Canada's ambassador to Peru, said there were about 15 rebels -- 13 men and two women. "Possibly there might be others, I don't know."
While decrying the methods used by the rebels to pursue their goals, he had praise for their restraint.
"Everybody so far, the hostages, the hostage-takers and the Peruvian government have shown a commendable degree of restraint," said the envoy, who will be returning to Lima.

"I hope it will end peacefully. We can't tell what's going to happen, but I think the fact that we got through this length of time without a really serious incident gives some cautious grounds for hope."
